design_detail: Record-linkage comparison of two state sources of poisoning deaths among New Mexico residents in 1995–1998. Source 1: vital statistics mortality files (death certificates; underlying cause coded in ICD-9 by nosologists trained by the National Center for Health Statistics (NCHS) in the state Office of Vital Records and Health Statistics; includes residents who died in another state). Source 2: the database of the statewide Office of the Medical Investigator (OMI), searched by OMI 'Manner of Death' codes that investigators assign when entering the death-certificate information developed by pathologists. Records were linked manually and deterministically (date of death, then age, sex, race or ethnicity and name; then allowing 1 day, 1 year and slight spelling differences), and unmatched poisonings were looked for among non-poisoning deaths in the other source. Three categories were counted four ways (vital statistics; OMI; both; either): all poisoning (ICD-9 305, E850–E869, E950–E952, E962, E980–E982), unintentional illicit drug overdose (E850.0, E854.2, E855.2, E858.8) and unintentional heroin overdose (E850.0, E858.8), the last two with and without E858.8, the code for accidental poisoning by 'other drugs' used when a certificate names drugs of different types. NCHS public-use multiple-cause files for 1995–1998, which could not be linked to individual records, showed which drug codes accompanied E858.8 in New Mexico and the US. Age-adjusted rates (1940 US standard) for 1989–1998. Descriptive; no reference standard and no statistical tests.
can_establish: How far two New Mexico sources agreed on which deaths of residents were poisonings, unintentional illicit drug overdoses and unintentional heroin overdoses in 1995–1998, why the discordant poisoning deaths differed (out-of-state deaths, deaths not reported to the medical investigator, certificate wording and coding rules), and how much the multi-drug code E858.8 changes subcategory counts.
cannot_establish: Which source was right about any discordant death (no independent review); the true number of heroin deaths (ICD-9 has no heroin-specific code and the OMI heroin category is not defined in the paper); how many deaths both sources missed; how far including E858.8 overcounts heroin deaths beyond the 55.6% that matched OMI morphine deaths; or whether the results hold under ICD-10 (in use from 1999) or in states without a centralized medical examiner.

sample.recruitment: Records: New Mexico vital statistics mortality files and the OMI database; all poisoning deaths of New Mexico residents occurring in 1995–1998 (pp. 274–275).
sample.inclusion_exclusion: Deaths of New Mexico residents, including out-of-state deaths in vital statistics. The OMI may investigate all sudden, unexplained, suspicious, violent or unattended deaths in New Mexico except within certain tribal and federal jurisdictions (Indian reservations and military installations), where it is often invited (p. 274). 'Poisoning' covers all agents, not drugs only: the definition takes ICD-9 305, E850–E869, E950–E952, E962 and E980–E982, and the authors describe poisoning as involving agents as diverse as carbon monoxide, alcohol, prescription drugs and drugs such as heroin and cocaine (Introduction, 3rd paragraph, and Materials and Methods › Definitions, 1st paragraph, p. 274); 7 of the 17 OMI poisonings coded as other injuries in vital statistics were fire-related (p. 276).
sample.demographics: Poisoning death rates 1995–1998: highest at ages 35–44 (33.5 per 100,000 person-years), then 25–34 (28.1); White Hispanic 20.8, White non-Hispanic 12.5, Native American 8.1 (lowest); men 22.2 against women 7.8 (sex and race or ethnicity rates age-adjusted). Intent: 78.3% unintentional, 21.2% suicide, 0.3% homicide, 0.2% undetermined (p. 275).
sample.attrition: Not applicable (records). The 24 out-of-state deaths among the discordant vital-statistics poisonings were not reviewed further.
sample.selection_effects: One state with a centralized medical examiner, which the authors expect to capture more injury deaths than non-centralized medical examiner or coroner systems; deaths on tribal and federal land fall outside OMI jurisdiction unless it is invited. The authors work for the agencies that produce both sources.

exposure.measurement: How a death entered each count, and who decided. Vital statistics: the certifier's two-part cause-of-death section, coded by nosologists under explicit rules: 'use' or 'abuse' on the certificate gives ICD-9 305 (nondependent abuse of drugs); 'overdose', 'intoxication', 'toxicity' or 'poisoning' gives an external-cause E-code; a single drug in part I is coded as that drug even if part II lists others; several drugs of one type in part I are coded as that type (e.g., codeine, heroin and morphine as opiates, E850.0 when accidental); drugs of different types in part I are coded as E858.8 when accidental; drug plus alcohol is coded by the drug, alcohol alone in part I as alcohol; a natural condition in part I with a drug in part II is coded as the natural condition unless it is a direct sequel of drug use (p. 274). OMI: for all deaths suspected to be due to drugs, toxins or poisons a full autopsy and toxicological evaluation is carried out by policy (Toxicology Bureau of the New Mexico Scientific Laboratory Division; screening findings confirmed, e.g., by gas chromatography or mass spectrometry; antemortem specimens obtained when the person died after hospitalization), and pathologists consult the toxicologists (p. 274). The share of deaths actually autopsied and tested is not reported.
exposure.polysubstance: Central to the question: accidental poisonings naming drugs of different types are coded E858.8, which hides the drugs in underlying-cause data. Multiple-cause codes 965.0 (opiates and related narcotics), 968.5 (surface and infiltration anaesthetics, including cocaine) and 969.7 (psychostimulants, including amphetamines) were used to see what lay behind E858.8.

comparison.controls: The two sources compared with each other. Percentages are of the deaths found in either source ('captured by either database'), not of an independent reference.

outcomes.instruments: Counts by year and in total for each source, both and either (Tables 1–3, pp. 276–277); review of discordant poisoning deaths (p. 276); shares of E858.8 deaths matched to OMI drug codes (p. 276); multiple-cause code frequencies (pp. 276–277); age-adjusted rates (Figure 1, p. 276).
outcomes.validity_norms: Neither source is validated; OMI Manner of Death codes were developed for data retrieval, and the OMI definitions of illicit drug and heroin overdose are not given.
outcomes.operationalization: Categories as in the design; a death is 'captured' by a source if it is in that source's category, among deaths in either source's category.
outcomes.assessor_blinding: Not reported; who linked and reviewed the records is not stated.

analysis.effect_sizes: Poisoning: vital statistics 1,046 and OMI 1,046 of 1,105 deaths in either source (94.7% each); both 987 (89.3%). Discordant vital-statistics poisonings (59): 24 out of state; of the other 35, 13 (37.1%) not reported to the OMI, 15 (42.8%) OMI natural deaths coded 305 in vital statistics, 2 miscoded as non-poisoning by the OMI, 3 undetermined-intent poisonings classed otherwise by the OMI, 2 unintentional injuries of unspecified cause in the OMI. Discordant OMI poisonings (59): 4 (6.8%) not found in vital statistics, 1 revised OMI certificate not recoded, 17 (28.8%) coded as other injuries, 37 (62.7%) coded as natural deaths, 16 (43.2%) of these as heart disease (ICD-9 420–429). Illicit drug overdose with E858.8: vital statistics 609, OMI 526, both 494, either 640 (95.2%, 82.2%, 77.2%); without E858.8: vital statistics 339, both 277, either 480 (70.6%). Heroin overdose with E858.8: vital statistics 537, OMI 360, both 351, either 537 (100%, 67.0%, 65.4%); without E858.8: vital statistics 273, both 216, either 416. E858.8 deaths matched to an OMI death with a drug code for morphine, cocaine and/or methamphetamine: 72%; to an OMI illicit drug overdose with a morphine code: 55.6%. E858.8 deaths with multiple-cause code 965.0, 968.5 and/or 969.7: 90% New Mexico, 88% US; with 965.0: 85% and 83%. Editors' calculations: the number of E858.8 deaths is not printed; Tables 2 and 3 imply 270 and 264; Table 3's union omits 9 OMI-only heroin deaths (reporting issues).
analysis.covariates: Rates age-adjusted to the 1940 US standard population; no other adjustment.
analysis.selective_reporting: Discordant illicit drug and heroin deaths are not reviewed case by case as the poisoning deaths were; the number of E858.8 deaths and the OMI heroin definition are not given.

interpretation_gap.results_show: Linking New Mexico vital statistics and medical examiner (OMI) records for residents' poisoning deaths in 1995–1998, each source alone held 1,046 of the 1,105 deaths found in either (94.7%), and 987 (89.3%) were in both. Discordance ran both ways: of 59 vital-statistics poisonings not classed as poisonings by the OMI, 24 were out-of-state deaths, 13 were never reported to the OMI and 15 were OMI natural deaths that vital statistics coded to nondependent abuse of drugs (ICD-9 305, the code the coding rules give when 'use' or 'abuse' is written on the certificate; the certificates' words are not reported); of 59 OMI poisonings not classed as poisonings in vital statistics, 37 had been coded as natural deaths (typically with poisoning mentioned only in part II of the certificate) and 17 as other injuries. Subcategory counts hinge on E858.8: with it, vital statistics held 95.2% of illicit drug and 100% of heroin deaths found in either source, the OMI 82.2% and 67.0%; without it, vital statistics held 70.6% of illicit drug deaths (as printed).
interpretation_gap.claimed: (1) The abstract says each source alone captured smaller percentages of illicit drug and heroin deaths; this holds for the OMI and, for vital statistics, only without E858.8 (reporting issue 5). (2) 'Captured' measures overlap with the union of two imperfect definitions, not accuracy: ICD-9 has no heroin-specific code, as the authors concede (p. 278); the vital-statistics heroin definition (E850.0 or E858.8) admits other opiates and mixtures; and 44.4% of E858.8 deaths did not match an OMI illicit drug overdose with a morphine code (editors' calculation from 55.6%), so the union contains deaths that were not heroin deaths and the OMI's 67.0% understates its completeness by an unknown amount. (3) The recommendation to include E858.8 in illicit drug and heroin definitions (p. 278) trades undercounting for overcounting; by the paper's own figures 10–12% of E858.8 deaths are not due to illicit drugs, and more are not due to heroin, which the Discussion does not weigh. (4) 'Illicit drugs' in the multiple-cause analysis are codes 965.0, 968.5 and 969.7, which by the paper's own descriptions include opiates and related narcotics, surface and infiltration anaesthetics and psychostimulants, so the 90% and 88% are upper bounds for illicit drugs. (5) The Results' statement that all three New Mexico rates were substantially higher than the US poisoning rate after 1993 does not fit Figure 1 for heroin (reporting issue 6).

timeline.event: Soslow and Wolf (Massachusetts, ref 10) and, in 1994, Dijkhuis et al. (ref 9): cited for medical examiner records capturing an inadequate share of poisoning and injury deaths (p. 274); not read for this card.

Moolenaar et al. (ref 11): New Mexico carbon monoxide deaths 1980–1988, medical examiner against national mortality data; cited for New Mexico's centralized medical examiner capturing most injury deaths (p. 274); not read for this card.
Hoppe-Roberts et al. (ref 6): poison control centre reports capture only 5% of poisoning deaths, as cited (p. 274); not read for this card.
Ossiander: textual cause-of-death data used to study drug poisoning deaths; listed for this page, not read for this card.

Horon et al. (Maryland, 2012–2015; card sc_horon_2018): certificates naming heroin identified 1,130 overdose deaths against 2,182 found by a protocol adding toxicology markers and scene evidence from the medical examiner's records.

Stam et al. (Victoria, 2012–2013, ICD-10; card sc_stam_2019): the largest shortfall of heroin-coded deaths against coronial records was under X44, accidental poisoning by other and unspecified drugs (69 against 98), a comparable non-specific code.

replication.where_it_stands: The problem identified here, multi-drug poisonings coded to a non-specific code that hides the drugs involved, recurs under ICD-10 in Victoria (card sc_stam_2019), and heroin deaths remain hard to identify from certificates alone in Maryland (card sc_horon_2018). The ICD-10 linkage of medical examiner and vital statistics records the authors called for is not among the papers read for this card.

funding.declared_conflicts: Not reported: the article has no conflict-of-interest statement.
funding.affiliations_note: Authors from the New Mexico Department of Health (Office of Epidemiology; Office of Vital Records and Health Statistics; Public Health Division) and the Office of the Medical Investigator, University of New Mexico School of Medicine, that is, the agencies that produce both data sources (p. 273). Recorded as a flag for closer reading.

what_would_settle_it: Linking medical examiner case files, with their toxicology results, to ICD-10 underlying- and multiple-cause records for the same deaths, with blinded pathologist review of samples in both directions (deaths coded as heroin or illicit-drug poisoning that were not, and deaths with heroin evidence that were not so coded), would measure the accuracy of each definition rather than their overlap.

domains.domain: 1. Sample frame appropriate to the target population
domains.note: Statewide vital statistics (including out-of-state deaths of residents) and the statewide medical examiner database are the right frames for residents' poisoning deaths.
All poisoning deaths in both sources, 1995–1998; no sampling.
1,105 poisoning deaths; 640 illicit drug and 537 heroin deaths in either source.

domains.domain: 4. Study subjects and setting described in detail
domains.note: Rates by age, sex, race or ethnicity and intent; both systems and the coding rules are described in detail.

domains.domain: 5. Data analysis with sufficient coverage of the identified sample
domains.note: Discordant poisoning deaths were reviewed one by one, except 24 out-of-state deaths; discordant illicit drug and heroin deaths were not reviewed, and the printed heroin union leaves out 9 OMI-only deaths.

domains.domain: 6. Valid methods for identifying the condition
domains.note: Poisoning is identified by two established systems, but ICD-9 has no heroin code, E850.0 and E858.8 include other drugs, the OMI heroin category is not defined, and neither source is checked against a reference.

domains.domain: 7. Condition measured in a standard, reliable way across participants
domains.note: Nosologists follow explicit NCHS rules and the OMI has autopsy and confirmed-toxicology policies, but the linkage was manual with no error rate, and the multiple-cause records could not be linked.
Counts and percentages are appropriate and mostly consistent, but union columns in Tables 2 and 3 are internally inconsistent (one value impossible) and no uncertainty is given.

domains.domain: 9. Adequate response rate, or low rate managed

risk_of_bias.reasoning: JBI-prevalence fits a comparison of death counts from two registers (round brief, record-linkage studies). The poisoning comparison is careful (manual linkage and case-by-case review of discordant deaths in both directions); the illicit drug and heroin comparisons rest on non-specific ICD-9 codes, an undefined OMI category and union columns with arithmetic errors. Citable for: in New Mexico in 1995–1998 vital statistics and medical examiner records each held about 95% of residents' poisoning deaths found in either; deaths were lost from vital-statistics poisoning counts when they were coded as natural deaths, typically with poisoning only in part II of the certificate, and added when deaths the medical examiner classed as natural were coded 305, the code the rules give for 'use' or 'abuse' on the certificate (the certificates' words are not reported); 'poisoning' here covers all agents, including alcohol and carbon monoxide; the multi-drug code E858.8 holds a large share of illicit drug and heroin deaths in underlying-cause data. Not citable for: the accuracy of either source, the true number of heroin deaths, or the 70.6% figure without its caveat.

key_findings.finding: Poisoning deaths of New Mexico residents, 1995–1998: 1,046 in vital statistics, 1,046 in OMI records, 987 in both and 1,105 in either; each source alone held 94.7% and both together 89.3% of the deaths in either. By year, either source: 255, 249, 289 and 312; deaths rose by all four approaches each year from 1996 to 1998.
Only vital statistics held New Mexico residents who died in another state: 24 poisoning deaths over the 4 years.

Of 59 poisoning deaths in vital statistics not classed as poisonings by the OMI, 24 occurred out of state and were not reviewed; of the other 35, 13 (37.1%) were never reported to the OMI; 15 (42.8%) were natural deaths in the OMI database (e.g., cirrhosis, sepsis, heart disease) that vital statistics attributed to nondependent drug abuse (ICD-9 305); 2 were miscoded as non-poisoning by the OMI; 3 were undetermined-intent poisonings in vital statistics classed differently by the OMI; 2 were unintentional injuries of unspecified cause in the OMI.

Of 59 OMI poisoning deaths not classed as poisonings in vital statistics, 4 (6.8%) were not found in vital statistics; 1 had a revised OMI certificate that was not recoded; 17 (28.8%) were coded as other injury deaths (6 unintentional fire-related deaths, 1 fire-related suicide); 37 (62.7%) were coded as natural deaths, typically with poisoning mentioned in part II but not part I of the certificate; 16 (43.2%) of these were coded as heart disease (ICD-9 420–429).

Unintentional illicit drug overdose deaths: with E858.8, vital statistics 609, OMI 526, both 494, either 640, so vital statistics held 95.2% and the OMI 82.2% of the deaths in either; without E858.8, vital statistics 339, both 277, either 480, so vital statistics held 70.6%.
key_findings.note: The excluding-E858.8 union is internally inconsistent (reporting issue 1); with the OMI counts from the left half of Table 2 the union would be 588 and vital statistics would hold about 58% (editors' calculation).

key_findings.finding: Unintentional heroin overdose deaths: with E858.8, vital statistics 537, OMI 360, both 351, either 537, so vital statistics held 100% and the OMI 67.0%; without E858.8, vital statistics 273, both 216, either 416.
key_findings.note: The printed union (537) leaves out the 9 OMI heroin deaths that were not in vital statistics (360 − 351); with them, vital statistics would hold 98.4% and the OMI 65.9% (editors' calculation; reporting issue 2).

key_findings.finding: Of vital-statistics deaths coded E858.8, 72% matched an OMI death with a drug code for morphine, cocaine and/or methamphetamine, and 55.6% matched an OMI illicit drug overdose with a drug code for morphine.
key_findings.locator: Results, 3rd paragraph (starts on p. 275; the 72% sentence is on p. 276) and 4th paragraph (p. 276)
key_findings.note: The number of E858.8 deaths is not printed; both percentages fit 270 deaths (e.g., 150/270 = 55.6%; editors' calculation).

key_findings.finding: In NCHS multiple-cause data, 90% of New Mexico resident deaths and 88% of US deaths with underlying cause E858.8 also carried code 965.0 (opiates and related narcotics), 968.5 (surface and infiltration anaesthetics, including cocaine) and/or 969.7 (psychostimulants, including amphetamines); 85% and 83% carried 965.0. The authors conclude that 10–12% of E858.8 deaths are not due to illicit drugs.

Coding rules that decide whether and how a drug death is counted in vital statistics: 'use' or 'abuse' on the certificate gives ICD-9 305; 'overdose', 'intoxication', 'toxicity' or 'poisoning' gives an external-cause code; several drugs of one type in part I are coded as that type, drugs of different types as E858.8 (accidental) or the corresponding suicide, homicide or undetermined codes; drug plus alcohol is coded by the drug; a natural condition in part I with a drug only in part II is coded as the natural condition unless it is a direct sequel of drug use.
key_findings.locator: Materials and Methods › Definitions, 2nd to 4th paragraphs

key_findings.finding: The OMI investigates sudden, unexplained, suspicious, violent or unattended deaths statewide except within certain tribal and federal jurisdictions; for all deaths suspected to be due to drugs, toxins or poisons it carries out a full autopsy and toxicological evaluation, with screening results confirmed (e.g., gas chromatography or mass spectrometry) and antemortem specimens obtained for people who died after hospitalization.
key_findings.locator: Materials and Methods › Data sources › Medical examiner records

key_findings.finding: Timeliness: the OMI typically reported in-state poisoning deaths within 3 months of death; underlying-cause vital statistics were typically available within 1 year after the calendar year, with classification more consistent under explicit coding rules; NCHS public-use multiple-cause data about 2 years after.

Recommendations: surveillance should use medical examiner data, underlying-cause and multiple-cause vital statistics; E858.8 should be included in definitions of unintentional illicit drug and heroin overdose deaths; the illicit drug category should consist of E850.0 (opiates and related narcotics), E854.2 (psychostimulants: amphetamines and caffeine), E855.2 (local anaesthetics: cocaine, lidocaine, procaine and tetracaine) and E858.8. The authors note that no ICD-9 or ICD-10 code corresponds exactly to unintentional heroin overdose.

New Mexico rates of poisoning, unintentional illicit drug overdose and unintentional heroin overdose rose in 1989–1998 (Figure 1, age-adjusted to the 1940 US population); poisoning in New Mexico was above the US poisoning rate throughout. Values are not printed and were not extracted.

Limitations stated by the authors: the NCHS multiple-cause files could not be linked to the linked medical examiner and underlying-cause records; the study used ICD-9 data, ICD-10 being used from 1999 deaths, so a similar ICD-10 study is needed.

reporting_issues.issue: Table 2, excluding E858.8: the 1998 union ('VS or OMI', 108) is smaller than the vital-statistics count for the same year ('VS only', 109), which is impossible for a union. Editors' calculation with the OMI counts from the left half of the table: the 1995 and 1996 unions (123, 121) are reproduced, but 1997 and 1998 would be 134 and 210, and the total 588 rather than 480.
reporting_issues.consequence: The text's 70.6% (339 of 480) depends on the inconsistent total; with 588 the vital-statistics share without E858.8 would be about 58%. The direction of the conclusion (excluding E858.8 loses many deaths) is unchanged.

reporting_issues.issue: Table 3, including E858.8: the union of the two sources equals the vital-statistics count (537), although 9 OMI heroin deaths (360 − 351; 5 in 1995, 2 in 1996, 2 in 1997) were not in the vital-statistics count (editors' calculation).
reporting_issues.consequence: The 100% and 67.0% are computed on a denominator that leaves out OMI-only heroin deaths; with them the shares would be 98.4% and 65.9% (editors' calculation).

reporting_issues.issue: One-death discrepancies in the union columns (editors' calculation): Table 2 (with E858.8) gives a 1997 union of 151 and a total of 640, where the columns give 152 and 641; Table 3 (without E858.8) gives a 1997 union of 91 and a total of 416, where the columns give 92 and 417.
reporting_issues.consequence: Minor; percentages change by less than a tenth of a point.

reporting_issues.issue: The vital-statistics columns imply different numbers of E858.8 deaths in the two tables, although both definitions include every unintentional E858.8 death (editors' calculation): 609 − 339 = 270 in Table 2 against 537 − 273 = 264 in Table 3; by year, 45 against 43 in 1995 and 72 against 68 in 1997.
reporting_issues.consequence: At least one vital-statistics count is wrong by up to 6 deaths; the number of E858.8 deaths, the denominator of the 72% and 55.6%, is never printed.

reporting_issues.issue: The abstract states that for illicit drug and heroin overdose deaths each source alone captured smaller percentages than for poisoning (94.7%); with E858.8 included, Tables 2 and 3 give vital statistics 95.2% and 100%. The Results also describe either source as capturing 5.4% more poisoning deaths than either alone (editors' calculation: 59 more deaths are 5.6% of 1,046 or 5.3% of 1,105).
reporting_issues.consequence: The abstract's statement holds only for the OMI, and for vital statistics only when E858.8 is excluded.

reporting_issues.issue: The Results say the New Mexico rates of poisoning, illicit drug overdose and heroin overdose were all substantially higher than the US poisoning rate after 1993; in Figure 1, read enlarged (no values printed; years from the axis), the heroin overdose rate lies below the US poisoning rate in 1994 and at about the same level in 1996 and 1997, and the illicit drug overdose rate is at about the US level in 1994.
reporting_issues.consequence: Only the New Mexico poisoning rate was clearly above the US rate in every year after 1993; the figure also compares New Mexico subcategories with total US poisoning, which are not like for like.
